indicators.note: something amazing leaves you bewildered, so the letters are thrown into confusion
about can mean turned around or moved here and there, a second hint that letters move

explanation.surface: A puzzler marvels at an acrostic poem written about some nation.
explanation.walkthrough: The article 'a' does double duty: it is part of the fodder as well as reading as part of the definition 'a country'.
explanation.definitionFit: Costa Rica is a Central American nation, so it is an example of a country.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the board game of kings, queens and checkmate
second meaning: a stage musical by the ABBA songwriters with Tim Rice

explanation.walkthrough: 'Game show' reads as one television term, but it splits into two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The board game and the 1980s West End musical share the same title, so one word fits both halves.

indicators.note: something rebuilt is put together again in a new form, so the letters get a new order

explanation.surface: A religious group reconstructs its meeting place to show it off.
explanation.definitionFit: A spectacle is an impressive public display, a synonym for a show.

clue.text: Fashion trade company's style of interior design

indicators.note: to fashion is to shape or make, so the following word is reshaped

parts.note: CO is the standard abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: It reads like a description of a fashion firm's house look for interiors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fashion' looks like a noun about clothes, but it is the verb that reshapes the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: Art Deco is the geometric 1920s-30s decorative movement, much used in architecture and interiors.

clue.text: Banged up often, I'm close to parole, and not a moment too soon

parts.note: slang: in prison, the nick being British slang for jail
oft is the old word for often

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is kept

explanation.surface: A frequent prisoner, nearing release on parole, gets out just in time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banged up' and 'the nick' are both British slang for being in jail; the whole phrase IN THE NICK is one chunk.
explanation.definitionFit: In the nick of time is an idiom for at the last possible moment, just before it would be too late.

clue.text: Not knowing what to say, unable to go at Scrabble?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: speechless, stumped for a reply
second, playful meaning: a player who cannot form any word with their tiles

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second, literal reading: in Scrabble you are stuck when no word can be made.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means speechless; read literally it describes lacking playable words in a word game.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: acid or pungent in taste, or cutting in tone
second meaning: a musical note raised a semitone

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bitter note' sounds like a resentful letter, but the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Sharp describes a harsh acid taste and also names a raised note in music notation.

clue.text: Composer from Wales met an arranger

indicators.note: from says the letters are taken out of the run of words that follows

parts.note: spans the end of Wales, all of met an, and the start of arranger

explanation.surface: A Welsh musician meets a music arranger.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites a Welsh composer; the name runs across the word breaks instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedrich Smetana was the 19th-century Czech composer of Ma Vlast and The Bartered Bride.

clue.text: I start to support a married friend

indicators.note: in a down entry, what supports something sits beneath it, so these pieces come below the others

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for married
a go is a start or attempt, as in a fresh go

explanation.surface: Someone begins backing a married pal.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue lists the bottom half first: I and start sit under a married.
explanation.definitionFit: Amigo is the Spanish word for friend, used informally in English as a pal.

clue.text: Girl, possibly ten, describing a type of poker

indicators.note: to describe a circle is to draw round, so these pieces go round the next one
possibly suggests one way the letters might be arranged, not the given one

explanation.surface: A girl, perhaps aged ten, explains a kind of poker game.
explanation.walkthrough: The girl's name and the shuffled number together go round the letter from 'a', so it sits between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Penny-ante poker is played for very small stakes, hence also meaning trivial or small-time.

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A slot in the schedule reserved for each new instalment of a series.
explanation.definitionFit: An event is an occurrence or incident, a synonym for an episode in the sense of something that happens.

indicators.note: something terrible is a mess, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A performer who is awful at reading his lines.
explanation.definitionFit: A tragedian is a stage performer who specialises in tragic roles, a particular kind of actor.

clue.text: Defiant remark from habitual drunkard present

parts.note: a sot is a person who is regularly drunk

explanation.surface: A drunk at the scene answers back defiantly.
explanation.definitionFit: So there is an exclamation said to show stubborn triumph or defiance at the end of an argument.

clue.text: Speaker at rear of lady chapel

parts.note: an orator is a public speaker

indicators.note: the rear of a word is its back end, so only the last letter is used

explanation.surface: A preacher stands at the back of the church's Lady Chapel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lady chapel' reads as one church term, but the definition is chapel alone.
explanation.definitionFit: An oratory is a small chapel for private prayer, so the words are synonyms.

parts.note: a station is a stage or stopping point on a route

explanation.surface: A queen attends a stage performance at the theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stage play' looks like one phrase, but play alone is the definition; Victoria Station is also a London railway terminus.
explanation.definitionFit: Victoria Station is a short 1982 play by Harold Pinter about a taxi controller and a lost driver.

clue.text: Uncommonly civil about threesome, or biting

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the next piece sits inside
uncommonly suggests an unusual form, so the letters take an odd new order

parts.note: a trio is a group of three

explanation.surface: A puzzled diner asks whether a trio is unusually polite or rather sharp-tongued.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Civil' and 'biting' are opposites, which hides that the polite word is only fodder; vitriol is an old name for sulphuric acid.
explanation.definitionFit: Vitriolic means caustic and savage in criticism, like the acid vitriol, so it means biting in tone.

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters are knocked out of order

explanation.surface: A sad comment that idleness brings no decline at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Indolence is avoidance of effort or activity, a synonym for laziness.

clue.text: It bore forbidden fruit — in legend, fewer took bananas

indicators.note: bananas is slang for crazy, so the letters go wild

explanation.surface: In a myth, the forbidden fruit was apparently bananas, and fewer people took it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' seems to be the fruit, but it is slang for crazy and signals the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil bore the fruit Adam and Eve were forbidden to eat.

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A piece of work goes on display in a single exhibit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' reads like a container instruction, but here every word simply contributes its letters in order.
explanation.definitionFit: An opinion is a view one holds, as in 'in my view'.

clue.text: Weapon made from pine — hollow base missing

indicators.note: in a down entry the base is the bottom, so the last letter is lost

parts.note: to pine is to long for something
a bowl is a hollow or basin

explanation.surface: A weapon fashioned from pine wood with a hollowed-out base.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pine' looks like timber for a bow, but it is the verb meaning yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: The longbow was the tall English bow used at Agincourt, a weapon for shooting arrows.

parts.note: a candidate who is elected is in
British slang: a brief is a lawyer, especially a barrister

explanation.surface: A newly elected lawyer is asked to give the summing-up.
explanation.walkthrough: A brief is British slang for a barrister or defence lawyer.
explanation.definitionFit: In brief is an idiom meaning in a few words, which is how one sums up.

clue.text: Labour statesman getting head round onset of violence

indicators.note: round says one piece encircles another

parts.note: bean is slang for the head

indicators.note: the onset is the beginning, so only the first letter counts

explanation.surface: A Labour politician has his head turned at the first hint of violence.
explanation.walkthrough: Aneurin Bevan was the Welsh Labour minister who founded Britain's National Health Service.
explanation.definitionFit: Nye Bevan was a leading Labour Party politician of the 1940s and 50s.

parts.note: W is the abbreviation for western
an angle is a point of view on a subject

explanation.surface: Someone twists Western viewpoints to suit an agenda.
explanation.definitionFit: To wangle is to get something by trickery or clever scheming, so wangles means manipulates.

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece wraps round the next
first says only the initial letter of the word is used

explanation.surface: A singer is annoyed about a contralto's debut recording.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Record' sounds like a disc; here it is the tally of points in a game.
explanation.definitionFit: A score is a record of points made in a game, or to score is to record them.

indicators.note: an output is something produced or made, so the letters are made into something new

explanation.surface: A French scientist's production of oil changes from batch to batch.
explanation.definitionFit: Antoine Lavoisier was the 18th-century French scientist called the father of modern chemistry.

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the preceding word is read backwards

parts.note: a nib is the writing point of a pen

explanation.surface: An author is about to depart the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer' suggests a person, but it is the pen point. House, or housey-housey, is an old British name for bingo, and the winning shout.
explanation.definitionFit: Bingo was long called house or housey-housey in Britain, so house is an older name for the game.

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
anon is an old word for at once

explanation.surface: A vicar is caught out straight away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' only places one piece next to the other; in cricket scoring C stands for caught.
explanation.definitionFit: A canon is a member of the clergy attached to a cathedral chapter.

clue.text: Heels were broken in another place

indicators.note: something broken is in pieces, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone's shoe heels snapped somewhere else.
explanation.definitionFit: Elsewhere is an adverb meaning in or to some other place.
